articles.title: Psychology says children may copy a classmate they don't even like; here's why it happens
articles.summary: A child comes home from school complaining about a classmate. They say the other child is bossy, refuses to share or keeps breaking classroom rules.
articles.body: A child comes home from school complaining about a classmate. They say the other child is bossy, refuses to share or keeps breaking classroom rules. Yet, a few days later, the parent notices something unexpected. Their child has started using the same phrases, making similar gestures or behaving in ways they previously criticised.For parents, this can be confusing. If a child does not particularly like someone, why would they copy their behaviour?The answer may lie in how children learn from the people around them. Imitation is not always a sign of admiration, friendship or even conscious approval. Sometimes, children pick up behaviours because they are observing what happens in their social environment, trying to understand group expectations or learning what helps them fit in.Developmental psychology research suggests that imitation serves purposes beyond simply learning a new skill. Children's relationships with others, their sense of belonging and the behaviour they see around them can all influence what they choose to copy.Children do not always copy people because they like themParents often assume that children imitate their closest friends or the people they admire. While affection can influence imitation, it is not the only factor.A 2020 review published in Annual Review of Developmental Psychology, titled The Social Function of Imitation in Development, examined how imitation helps children form and maintain social relationships. Research reviewed by psychologist Harriet Over suggests that children can use imitation as a way to affiliate with others, signalling social connection and a willingness to participate in shared activities.This does not mean that every copied action is an attempt to make friends. Rather, imitation can be influenced by the social significance of the person being observed and the situation in which the behaviour occurs.Consider a child who dislikes a classmate's habit of making jokes during lessons. The child may still begin repeating those jokes after noticing that other classmates laugh or pay attention. What gets copied may not be the classmate's personality but a behaviour that appears to attract a response from the group.The distinction matters: children can learn from someone's behaviour without liking that person or approving of everything they do.When a child's behaviour is shaped by the groupSometimes, the influence comes not from one particular classmate but from the behaviour of several children.A study published in the Journal of Experimental Child Psychology in 2015, The influence of peers on the tendency of 3- and 4-year-old children to over-imitate, examined how young children copied actions demonstrated by other children.The researchers found that children who initially used an efficient way to complete a task could switch to copying unnecessary actions after seeing several peers perform them. The children did not continue reproducing those unnecessary actions when they later completed the task privately.The findings suggest that children's behaviour can be influenced by what a group appears to do, even when copying the group does not make a task more efficient.Although this experiment involved a puzzle task rather than children copying disliked classmates at school, it offers a useful insight into peer influence: the behaviour of a group can sometimes matter more than whether a particular action is useful.In a classroom, a child might start using a popular expression, adopting a particular way of reacting to a teacher or following a playground routine simply because several other children do the same thing. The behaviour may become familiar through repetition and social exposure.This is one reason parents should avoid assuming that every copied habit represents a deliberate choice to imitate a particular child.Why children may copy behaviour they know is not idealA more complicated situation arises when the behaviour being copied is disruptive, unkind or contrary to what a child has been taught at home.Research suggests that younger children can be particularly sensitive to group membership when learning how to behave.A 2021 study in the Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, Group influence on children's prosocial and antisocial behavior, examined how children aged five to six and eight to nine responded after observing members of a group engage in either prosocial behaviour, such as sharing, or antisocial behaviour, such as stealing.The study found that younger children showed a stronger tendency to favour their own group, while older children's responses were more sensitive to the behaviour they had observed. The findings suggest that children's responses to group membership and behaviour change as they develop.This research does not directly show that children copy classmates they dislike. However, it helps explain why social affiliation can sometimes compete with a child's understanding of what is right or wrong.For example, a young child may know that teasing is unkind but still laugh along when a group of classmates does it. Another child may repeat a rude expression heard at school without fully understanding its meaning or consequences.Children are learning to navigate several things at once: what adults expect, what their peers do and how their own actions affect their relationships. These influences do not always point in the same direction.Does copying mean a child wants to be like that classmate?Children may imitate a behaviour because it is noticeable, repeated frequently or associated with a particular social setting. They may also experiment with words, gestures and habits before deciding whether these fit their own preferences.A 2011 study published in Developmental Psychology, titled Imitation in young children: when who gets copied is more important than what gets copied, explored how social affiliation influenced preschoolers' imitation of adults performing a task.The research adds to evidence that imitation is not simply a mechanical response to watching an action. Social information about the person demonstrating the behaviour can affect what children reproduce.However, the study examined adults rather than disliked classmates, so its findings should not be treated as direct proof of why a child copies someone they do not like.The broader lesson is that imitation is socially influenced and context-dependent. A child might repeat a classmate's catchphrase because everyone recognises it, copy a gesture because it has become part of a classroom joke, or adopt a habit after seeing it repeatedly.None of these behaviours, by itself, proves that the child secretly admires the classmate, wants to become their friend or is being pressured by them.What parents can do when they notice this behaviourThe most useful response is to understand what the child is copying and why, rather than immediately focusing on the person they have copied.1. Ask about the behaviour without accusing the childInstead of asking, "Why are you behaving like that child?", try asking, "I noticed you have started saying that. Where did you hear it?" A neutral question gives the child room to explain without feeling that they must defend themselves or their classmate.2. Separate the child from the behaviourIf the child has started using an insulting expression, explain why the expression can hurt someone. Avoid labelling the classmate as a bad influence based on one incident. Children need help evaluating actions, not just categorising people as good or bad.3. Talk about group pressure in everyday languageFor an older child, a parent might ask, "If everyone in your class starts doing something, do you feel you have to do it too?" This opens a conversation about making independent choices without assuming that the child is deliberately following others.4. Notice what the behaviour achievesDoes the child repeat a joke because classmates laugh? Do they use a particular phrase because it gets attention? Or are they copying a routine that has become common in their classroom? Understanding the context can help parents decide whether the behaviour needs a conversation, a clear boundary or simply time to pass.5. Reinforce the values you want the child to practiseChildren benefit from specific guidance about kindness, respect, honesty and inclusion. Rather than only telling them whom not to copy, parents can help them consider how an action affects another person and what they could do differently.If the behaviour involves bullying, aggression, humiliation or persistent rule-breaking, it is important to address the behaviour directly and work with the school when necessary.The bigger parenting lessonA child copying a classmate they complain about is not necessarily being inconsistent. Children's social relationships are complicated, and their behaviour may be shaped by curiosity, familiarity, group expectations or a desire to participate in what is happening around them.Research on imitation and peer influence shows that children do not learn only from the people they love or admire. They also observe the wider social world and gradually work out which behaviours to adopt, reject or question.For parents, the goal is not to control every influence a child encounters. It is to help them develop the confidence to think about what they see, understand the consequences of their actions and make choices that reflect their own values - even when the people around them are doing something different.You use AI every day. articles.title: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
articles.summary: China is the North's largest trading partner and a lifeline against the sanctions Pyongyang faces.
articles.body:
A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours.

China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme.

The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them.

Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty.

The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region.

It is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges".

Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea.

A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC.

"Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds.

"China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually."

Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong.

But the alliance is not without tension.

Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan.

China's attitude has shifted more recently.

"Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC.

Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war.

At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops.

Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day.

So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties.

Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month.

Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

"The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.

"But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing."

articles.title: North Korea tests two submarine-launched missiles, state media reports
articles.summary: The tests showcase North Korea’s war deterrent capabilities in the region, KCNA says.
articles.body:
North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles in the sea off its east coast, state media KCNA reports.

The test-fire on Wednesday aimed to examine the reliability of war deterrents and improve the navy’s skill in performing strategic missions, the outlet said.

One of the missiles fired was a Pulhwasal-3-31, the same type of strategic cruise missile North Korea said it test-fired from land last week, according to KCNA.

Senior military officers observed the tests conducted at sea off the country’s east coast. KCNA added that the tests had no adverse impact on the security of neighbouring countries.

North Korea is not yet believed to have launched a modern missile submarine in full operation. This is a top military priority of the country’s leader Kim Jong Un, who has overseen the development of a range of strategic ballistic and cruise missiles.

Last year, Kim Jong Un criticised a nuclear submarine deal between the US and South Korea while he toured his country’s submarine production facility, where state media images showed an 8,700-tonne nuclear-powered missile submarine under construction. On his tour, he described the deal as a threat to the stability of the Korean Peninsula, KCNA reported.

Pyongyang has fired off a flurry of missiles in recent weeks.

Earlier this week, North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea off its east coast, adding to a series of tests as tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang are on the rise.

On October 3, North Korea also tested a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.

After the ballistic missile launch, Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff spokesperson Jang Do-young said the move appeared to be a show of force as it came days after South Korea tested its own hypersonic weapon.

Last week, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcase of a missile test by a South Korean president.

Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theatre of operations”.

Inter-Korean relations have further soured as a landmine blast , which Seoul blamed on North Korea, wounded three soldiers in September in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) between the two countries.

A joint South Korean-United Nations investigation concluded that two landmines that exploded last month in the DMZ were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago, prompting Seoul to demand an official apology.

Pyongyang has sharply accelerated military fortification along the DMZ as part of leader Kim Jong Un’s “hostile-states” policy, launched in 2023, to permanently sever ties with South Korea.

Diplomatic efforts on the Korean Peninsula have stalled since the collapse of denuclearisation talks between Washington and Pyongyang in 2019 during the first Trump administration. While Trump has floated the possibility of meeting Kim Jong Un in his second term, no such meeting has materialised.

articles.title: A former luxury steam yacht sank off San Francisco in 1920; researchers brought back the first underwater images using underwater robots
articles.summary: The Ituna was built in 1886 as a luxury steam yacht and was lost in 1920 while working as a steam trawler.
articles.body: The Ituna was built in 1886 as a luxury steam yacht and was lost in 1920 while working as a steam trawler. A gale struck north of the San Francisco Lightship station on 13 March 1920, and the 34-year-old vessel sank in 10 minutes. Twelve of the 14 crew members escaped, and two did not. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Office of National Marine Sanctuaries, sonar expert Gary Fabian has since used a remotely operated vehicle and an autonomous underwater vehicle to bring back what NOAA describes as the first underwater images of the shipwreck.How did the luxury steam yacht Ituna sink off San FranciscoThe Ituna was heading from San Francisco to Reedsport, Oregon, when the storm struck on 13 March 1920. The agency states that the seas split the ship's seams and flooded the forward hold, which plunged the vessel bow-first to the bottom of the ocean. The sinking took only 10 minutes.12 of the 14 crew members escaped and struggled for hours to keep their lifeboat afloat on the journey to the San Francisco Lightship. Two crew members were trapped in their bunks and went down with the ship. The vessel's cargo of machinery, bound for the Reedsport Fish Company, was valued at $30,000 at the time.What was the Ituna before it became a commercial fishing vesselNOAA states that the Ituna began life as a luxury steam yacht, built for John G. Mackie in 1886 by A. & J. Inglis in Glasgow, Scotland. It was named for the Latin name of the Solway Firth, the coastline border between England and Scotland. After several changes of ownership, it was bought by Allison V. Amour of Chicago, Illinois, whom NOAA describes as a wealthy socialite interested in natural sciences. In December 1894, the Ituna left New York for Havana and Mexico on a three-month scientific research expedition. The results were published as Archaeological Studies Among the Ancient Cities of Mexico, which scholars of Mesoamerican anthropology valued immensely.The vessel later became a first-class passenger cargo steamer, running between ports along the United States West Coast and Mexican ports under the flag of the Mexican Navigation and Commercial Company. Two years after that, it was purchased by the Frank E. Booth Canning Company of San Francisco and converted into a seagoing steam trawler. According to NOAA, it was one of the largest steam trawlers fishing off California's central coast and one of the first commercial fishing vessels to introduce the "otter trawl" to the Pacific coast, in 1918.Sonar technology helped identify the Ituna shipwreck off CaliforniaIts Office of National Marine Sanctuaries Maritime Heritage Program worked in partnership with Teledyne SeaBotix, Inc. and sonar expert Gary Fabian. The team used a remotely operated vehicle and an autonomous underwater vehicle to collect high-definition video footage, still images and side-scan sonar data for analysis. NOAA credits Cyril Poissonnett of Teledyne SeaBotix with deploying the autonomous underwater vehicle for the side-scan sonar survey of the Ituna.The images show the vessel's steel hull, which was designed by the yacht designer George Lennox Watson, as well as its triple expansion steam engine and its cargo of machinery. The agency reports that the clipper-ship bow of the former yacht provided identification of the wreck. NOAA adds that multiple marine species have colonised the shipwreck, including giant green anemones (Anthopleura xanthogrammica) and white plumose anemones (Metridium farcimen).How many shipwrecks lie beneath the Greater Farallones National Marine SanctuaryNearly 400 ships and aircraft wrecks lie on the seafloor of the recently expanded Greater Farallones National Marine Sanctuary and the nearby Golden Gate National Recreation Area, including four never-before-found vessels. The Maritime Heritage Program is engaged in a two-year study to discover and document these wrecks. 20 ships have been plotted so far, including the USS Independence and the freighter S.S. Selja.NOAA quotes Robert Schwemmer, West Coast Regional Maritime Heritage Coordinator, as saying the Ituna's story is an example of "the rich maritime legacy that rests beneath the waves of San Francisco Bay." Schwemmer also states that mapping and examining the wrecks is a key part of preserving them for future generations. He says exploration allows researchers to learn about the past of the United States as a seafaring nation and to test recent advances in technology that will help protect these marine resources.You use AI every day. articles.title: DAY 5 SKANDAMATA: A Mother Who Lets the Child Lead
articles.summary: When a child takes the first step away from the mother, muscles contract, nerves fire and the heart quietly adjusts.
articles.body: When a child takes the first step away from the mother, muscles contract, nerves fire and the heart quietly adjusts. Inside almost every cell, mitochondria convert energy from food into ATP, the usable currency that powers movement, thought and life. These tiny powerhouses carry an intimate signature: in human beings, mitochondrial DNA is ordinarily inherited from the mother.Biology has written a maternal memory into every step.Skandamata holds the young Skanda upon her lap. One day he will become the commander of the divine forces. Yet she does not hold him in order to remain indispensable. She holds him until he can stand, and then allows the strength she nurtured to acquire its own direction.The familiar description of mitochondria as the powerhouse of the cell contains a deeper lesson. A powerhouse does not create energy from nothing; it transforms available energy into a form that can be used. Motherhood often performs the same quiet alchemy. A child’s possibility may already exist, but love, nourishment, correction and trust help convert possibility into capacity.Modern biology has also changed the old picture of mitochondria as motionless, bean-shaped batteries. They form dynamic networks, continually joining, separating and adjusting to the cell’s needs. Living power is not rigid. It knows when to connect, when to divide and when to change its form. A wise mother, teacher or mentor does the same: holding close when protection is needed, loosening the hand when independence must begin.The Rigveda offers a vast vision of motherhood through Aditi, who is described as mother, father, son and all that has been or will be born. The maternal principle is therefore larger than gender. It is the sacred capacity to contain life without imprisoning it.In the Devi Sukta, the Mother declares, “Whom I choose, I make powerful; I make that person a knower, a seer, wise.” Divine power does not remain secure by keeping others weak. It reveals itself by awakening strength in another.The Durga Saptashati carries the same truth into battle. When the devas are defeated, their separate radiances come together to form the Goddess. Each then offers her a weapon. Victory becomes possible when guarded powers are released into a shared purpose. No one loses light by contributing to a greater flame.On the fifth day, think of one person whose inner powerhouse you can strengthen. Share knowledge without demanding imitation. Open a door without deciding the path beyond it. Speak someone’s name where opportunity is being discussed. Step aside when their turn arrives.Skandamata does not disappear when Skanda leaves her lap. She becomes present in his courage. The child walks ahead, carrying the mother’s inheritance in the energy of every step.Perhaps the deepest form of motherhood is this: to become less visible while making another life more capable. Love has not vanished. It has simply changed its address.Authored by: Dr Shambo Samrat Samajdar and Dr Shashank R Joshi

articles.title: Tamil Nadu team wins Mitsubishi Electric’s global competition
articles.summary: The team of Tharanika K, Seralathan R, Vijay B and Tharana A S from Sona College of Technology in Salem, Tamil Nadu, won the grand prize at the MECA
articles.body: The team of Tharanika K, Seralathan R, Vijay B and Tharana A S from Sona College of Technology in Salem, Tamil Nadu, won the grand prize at the MECA Global Finals 2026, a factory automation competition organised by Mitsubishi Electric in Tokyo last month. They won against competitors from engineering colleges in South Korea, Japan, Taiwan, Vietnam, Philippines and Thailand. Normally, programming a factory machine’s controller (PLC) is slow and risky. Engineers write code by hand and can test it once the physical machine exists. This causes delays, needs scarce specialist programmers, and makes mistakes expensive to fix. Tharanika and team built a tool that lets an engineer describe a factory machine’s behaviour in plain English, and AI turns that description into working programmable logic controller (PLC) code. AI converts the machine instructions into safety-checked industrial code, and tests it on a digital twin before deployment, enabling quick development, safer validation, fewer programming errors, and reduced time, cost and effort during on-site commissioning.Seralathan told us their win could have been because their idea is potentially scalable across all kinds of PLCs – unlike the more narrow use cases of competing teams – and their use of an infrequently used programming language for AI to work on top of.The India leg of the competition saw nearly 300 applications from engineering colleges. In this leg, the second and third prize winners were respectively MKSSS’ Cummins College of Engineering for Women, Pune, and COEP Technological University, Pune.At the global level, the second and third prize winners were from Philippines and Thailand respectively.Atsushi Takase, MD of Mitsubishi Electric India, said the idea of the challenge was to empower the next generation of engineers by providing students with access to advanced automation technologies and opportunities to compete and excel on the global stage.You use AI every day. articles.summary: After an overnight vigil at India Gate, a pre-dawn swoop by Delhi Police brought the dharna for “Justice to Ankita Bhandari” to an end.
articles.body: After an overnight vigil at India Gate, a pre-dawn swoop by Delhi Police brought the dharna for “Justice to Ankita Bhandari” to an end. The cops arrived at the protest site at 4 am and took away the wailing parents of Ankita Bhandari, victim of rape and murder in Uttarakhand in 2022.Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and, later, AICC general secretary KC Venugopal visited the protest site on Wednesday evening to express solidarity with the parents. After they left, scores of Congress MPs, MLAs and workers of the Youth Congress and NSUI, among others, joined the dharna. Uttarakhand MLA and Congress office-bearer Qazi Nizamuddin, MPs Pawan Khera, Jothi Mani and Imran Pratapgarhi, Congress spokespersons Supriya Shrinate, Gurdeep Sappal and Ragini Nayak, Youth Congress president Uday Bhanu Chib, NSUI president Vinod Jakhar and Mahila Congress president Alka Lamba, among others, joined the vigil, which continued until early morning before being disrupted by the cops.Videos of the police action went viral, with Chib, Jakhar and others even trying to intercept the bus carrying the detainees.Ankita’s parents arrived from Uttarakhand on Wednesday evening and sat on a dharna along with activist Yogita Bhayana, holding a placard that read, “Stop protecting the VIP”. The continuing controversy over Ankita’s murder received a fresh lease of life with the appointment of BJP leader Dushyant Gautam as governor.The controversy revolves around the “VIP” who had allegedly sought “special service” at the infamous resort then owned by the son of a BJP leader. Ankita resisted the pressure. Her body was found in a canal in 2022, leading to a murder case.In a social media post, the Congress said there were allegations that Gautam was the “VIP” in question. “Narendra Modi has rewarded Gautam with the governorship of Sikkim. The girls and women of the country are watching how Modi and his govt are protecting Gautam. articles.title: Sourav Joshi called ‘misogynist’: YouTuber faces backlash after wife Avantika Bhatt is dared to drink from pet dog Oreo’s bowl
articles.summary: A joke in a family vlog has landed popular YouTuber Sourav Joshi in the middle of an online controversy.
articles.body: A joke in a family vlog has landed popular YouTuber Sourav Joshi in the middle of an online controversy. In a clip that is now doing the rounds on social media, his wife, Avantika Bhatt, is dared to drink water from their pet dog Oreo’s bowl during a game of truth or dare.The people playing the game seemed to take it lightly. But many viewers weren't amused. Some questioned the hygiene aspect, while others felt the challenge was in poor taste and asked why Avantika was put in that position in the first place.The video has also caught the attention of Amit Kilhor, a prominent Indian UPSC educator, mentor and content creator who founded Resolve IAS. Reacting to the episode, Kilhor called Sourav a misogynist, adding to the criticism the YouTuber is facing.What happened during the game?The clip comes from a vlog featuring Sourav and family members, including Piyush and Sahil. They were playing a bottle-spinning game when it was Avantika's turn to take on a challenge.After she chose a dare, Sourav asked her to drink water from Oreo's bowl. The exchange was treated as a joke, with comments such as “ek ghoot peena hai bas” and “saaf pani hai” suggesting that she only needed to take one sip and that the water was clean.That explanation, however, hasn't stopped the criticism.As the clip spread, viewers questioned the choice of dare. For some, it was simply unhygienic. Others felt that asking Avantika to drink from a dog's bowl was an unnecessary way to get a reaction on camera.And while truth or dare is meant to involve challenges, not everyone watching felt this one was funny.Amit Kilhor's reaction adds to the controversyAmit Kilhor also reacted to the video, calling Sourav a misogynist. Kilhor, who mentors UPSC aspirants and runs Resolve IAS, criticised the YouTuber over the incident.His remarks have brought another question into the conversation: was this just a joke between family members, or was Avantika being made the subject of a challenge that viewers found disrespectful?The reaction has been divided, but the criticism is clear. Many viewers have taken issue with the idea of turning an uncomfortable dare into entertainment, especially when it involves a creator's spouse.Kilhor's comment is his assessment of Sourav's behaviour in the video. Whether others agree with that label or not, the clip has prompted people to question the choice of challenge.Why are viewers objecting to the dare?Anyone who has watched a truth-or-dare game knows that some challenges can be silly, embarrassing or downright strange. Often, that's the whole point. But a dare that gets laughs from the people in the room may not go down as well with thousands of people watching online.Here, the debate isn't just about whether the water was clean. It's about why drinking from a pet's bowl was considered an acceptable challenge at all.Family vloggers regularly share jokes, games and everyday moments with their audiences. That doesn't mean every moment will land as intended. Once a clip is out there, viewers can question what they see, and a joke can quickly become a source of criticism.Some may feel the incident has been made into a bigger issue than it needs to be. Others believe the dare was unnecessary and that being part of a game doesn't automatically make it funny.For Sourav Joshi, a brief moment in a family vlog has now become a wider talking point, with viewers questioning the dare and Kilhor openly criticising his actions. What was presented as a bit of fun has clearly not been received that way by everyone.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: China’s $7.4 billion ‘loneliness’ industry: How modern life is turning companionship into a lucrative business
articles.summary: Living in a world where everyone’s supposedly a click away, it’s amazing, as well as a little sad, how hard it’s gotten to find real company.
articles.body: Living in a world where everyone’s supposedly a click away, it’s amazing, as well as a little sad, how hard it’s gotten to find real company. In China, this surprising gap is now fueling a booming business: The “loneliness industry,” which is a patchwork of services where companionship, emotional support, and basic human connection can be bought like any other product.Think about it. Whether people want someone to talk to, share a meal with, or just sit by their side, more and more are turning to paid-for relationships to fill the empty spots modern life leaves behind. It’s no longer just a private struggle or a phase people tough out alone. Now, for many, it’s a service they can find, book, and pay for, and it’s shaping a whole new market grounded in the realities of today’s urban isolation.In China, loneliness has an answer: It’s a $7.4 billion industryAs reported by Reuters earlier this year, numbers from Sinolink, a major Chinese securities firm, estimate that China’s loneliness industry hit $7.4 billion by 2025, and that figure could keep climbing. Demand has ballooned in recent years, even if nobody can put an exact number on every paid interaction or service. The reason is simple: As old forms of community break down and family ties get stretched by city living, work, or changing values, people are increasingly willing to open their wallets for a little less solitude.This isn’t just about “feeling sad.” It’s about a world where family structures have shrunk, friends are scattered, and crowds don’t always mean connection. All the while, entrepreneurs have spotted a need and are filling it; sometimes with simple conversation, sometimes with real, practical help.More than a listening ear: The faces of the loneliness economyThe human stories behind this trend really drive it home. Take 91-year-old Yang in suburban Beijing, as reported by the BBC Mirror. After her husband passed away and her eyesight got worse, Yang found herself so lonely she started talking to her TV for company. That changed when Wang Yingwei stepped in. He and his small delivery team started dropping by with hot meals and a helping hand for chores and household fixes. As the BBC reports, it’s not just about eating; it’s about seeing a friendly face, getting a little support, and feeling cared for. For Yang, and for others like Zheng Ruizhi, 75, Wang’s visits turned daily life from struggle to something a little more hopeful.Importantly, this whole industry isn’t just about trading cash for conversation. Sometimes, it fills a practical need when there’s no one else to step in. Elderly folks feel safer, more supported, and know someone’s got their back, even if it’s a paid arrangement.Why young professionals are buying companyAnd it’s not just the elderly. Young adults working far from home, often single and forging new lives far from the comfort of family or childhood friends, are fueling demand too. In big Chinese cities, work hours are long, making friends is tough, and getting through everyday tasks without a support system can be a tall order.The BBC profiled Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old who escorts clients to hospital appointments and picks up prescriptions. Some of her clients are young professionals who’d rather pay for this help than ask a work friend and risk owing a favor later. Cultural expectations play a big role here: If someone helps you, you’re expected to reciprocate. When you pay, you get help: no strings attached, and no awkward obligations.There are even hiking guides like Wang Zhoutao, a former soldier who leads hikes up China’s scenic mountains, snapping pictures, chatting, and providing a little moral support along the way. Businesses that started with a handful of companions now field hundreds; one outfit in Shandong, for example, provides paid hiking companions for about $116 a trip, and they’re rarely short on customers.More and more, people are willing to pay not just for activities, but for the experiences and emotional support that come with them. It marks a shift in how we think of consumption: purchasing the feeling, not just the product.Can you buy your way out of loneliness?There’s a reason paid companionship attracts people. Friendships take time, effort, and face the risk of rejection. Sometimes, people just want predictability; a clear price for a clear service. That’s what paid companions offer: no strings, no guessing.Psychotherapist Sami Wong told Reuters that knowing exactly what to expect, sans the emotional risk, makes these services appealing. There’s no rejection, and no pressure to emotionally invest unless you want to.But here’s where it gets complicated. Can a commercial transaction deliver the warmth, trust, and long-term support that real relationships give? Immediate company and practical help are valuable, sometimes lifesaving even. Jobs get done, fears ease, and loneliness fades, at least for a little while. But genuine relationships, with all their quirks, unpredictability, and mutual investment, are hard to replicate with money alone.And, of course, loneliness isn’t just about being physically alone. You can be surrounded by people or followers online, and still feel isolated.The booming business that’s built around a social problemChina’s loneliness economy isn’t happening in a vacuum. Urbanization means people leave home for work, social networks are pulled apart, and old models of “community” don’t always fit new lifestyles. Seniors want to age in place. Young people juggle high-pressure jobs and shifting family expectations. It’s no wonder companies offering support and companionship are booming.Research, like April 2026’s piece in The Atlantic, highlights how breakneck work culture, shrinking family circles, and the demands of big city life, especially for young professionals, make deep relationships difficult. Paid companions become more than a luxury; they’re a coping tool for a fast-changing social landscape.Of course, not all numbers are set in stone. The $7.4 billion number is more of an estimate than a definitive figure, as Reuters points out that getting a true measure of this industry is tricky, with so many services crossing lines between social, practical, and emotional help.The bottom lineChina’s loneliness industry reflects a big shift: Now more than ever, people are looking to buy the connection they can’t find organically. For the elderly and for young professionals alike, paid companionship can bring comfort, safety, and relief from isolation. However, deep down, this growing market is a mirror. It reflects the question everyone’s asking: why is it so much harder now to find the everyday care, attention, and genuine connection that makes us feel truly seen?Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: UK weather: Temperatures to rise to 23C before autumn chill sets in
articles.summary: Warm air will bring unseasonable warmth to the south and east of the UK on Thursday but chillier conditions are set to spread to all areas by the weekend.
articles.body:
Thursday will bring unusually high temperatures as warm air wafts across the south of the UK, while colder conditions dig into northern areas.

Afternoon highs in parts of eastern England are likely to be about 5-8C (9-14F) above typical mid-October values, probably peaking at 23C (73F).

It will be a different story further north and west with temperatures in much of Scotland and Northern Ireland sitting around the seasonal norm.

The two air masses are divided by a weather front which will bring outbreaks of rain. As that sinks southwards, chillier air will spread to all parts of the country bringing a colder feel to the weekend, though there will still be plenty of sunshine.

Frost and patchy fog are likely to develop in some locations.

A weather front that has already brought rain to Scotland and Northern Ireland will edge slowly southwards on Thursday, meaning a soggy afternoon for northern England, Wales and parts of south-west England.

To the south-east of the rain band, brisk southerly winds caused by a very deep area of low pressure passing close to Iceland will continue to feed warm air across many central, eastern and southern parts of England.

Sunny spells in these areas will lift temperatures to 19-23C (66-73F) making it feel unseasonably warm for late October.

As the rain band clears from northern parts of the UK, Scotland and Northern Ireland will turn mostly sunny with blustery winds and scattered heavy showers.

Afternoon highs here will be around 12-15C (54-59F) and these chillier conditions will be a sign of things to come for the whole of the UK, with colder air set to spread southwards by Friday and linger into the weekend.

High pressure will take charge of the weather for the end of the week providing sunny spells in many areas.

A few showers are also possible - especially in the north and west of the UK on Friday, then in the south-east of England over the weekend.

As the high builds from the west, widespread northerly winds will develop delivering colder air and a chilly feel.

Daytime temperatures will end up near the October average, ranging from 10 to 16C (50-61F) across the UK, although it will feel colder than that where winds turn blustery - particularly along the coasts of eastern Scotland and eastern England.

The nights will also turn cold with single-digit lows in almost all areas and the chance of a touch of frost as well as some patchy mist and fog.

Thermometers are likely to dip below freezing in some locations in Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England.

For some places it could be the coldest weather of the autumn so far but it is worth noting that these temperatures are not unusual for this time of year.

There is a lot of uncertainty about the forecast for next week with conflicting signals from computer weather models.

High pressure is likely to remain close to the UK initially but there are signs that Atlantic weather systems will eventually break through, powered by the jet stream , bringing a return to wetter, windier and somewhat milder conditions.

However, there is uncertainty about how quickly that change will take place so it is worth keeping an eye on the BBC Weather website and app .

You can read our latest thoughts on the forecast even further ahead in our monthly outlook .
